$comment: What the installer's component picker offers (#640). Six entries: the
five download clients Deluno's dispatcher recognises
(Deluno.Connections.DownloadClientProtocolCatalog carries the same five
keys) and Weir.
Every entry here runs the VENDOR'S OWN installer as its own process. Deluno
never merges these into its own payload, and never installs anything a box
was left unticked for.
sha256 is filled in the same way rig-software.json fills it: staged once,
hashed once, then pinned so every later run refuses a file that does not
match, rather than trust-on-first-use of whatever the URL answers with
today. An entry with mustBeSigned instead relies on the file's own
Authenticode signature, verified against the publisher name at install
time -- for a vendor whose Windows build changes often enough that pinning
a single version would mean shipping installers that go stale.
Weir has neither: it publishes SHA256SUMS.txt with every GitHub release,
next to Weir-win-Setup.exe, so its own release is verified against its own
published checksum instead of one pinned in this file. See
resolveUrl/resolveChecksum below.
Licence text is not duplicated here. licenceUrl points at each project's
own licence, shown by the picker before anything is downloaded (#640 item 7).

qbittorrent.configFileContent:
[Preferences]
WebUI\Enabled=true
WebUI\Port=8081
WebUI\Address=*
WebUI\LocalHostAuth=false
WebUI\AuthSubnetWhitelistEnabled=true
WebUI\AuthSubnetWhitelist=127.0.0.1/32
WebUI\CSRFProtection=false
WebUI\HostHeaderValidation=false

[LegalNotice]
Accepted=true
qbittorrent.note: qBittorrent's default Web UI port (8080) is given to SABnzbd instead, since both default there and only one can bind it; qBittorrent moves to 8081. A clean-VM run showed the Web UI never answered on 8081: qBittorrent (portable=false) reads its settings from %AppData%\qBittorrent\qBittorrent.ini (Roaming), not %LocalAppData% -- the previous seed path wrote a file qbittorrent.exe never looked at, so it always started with WebUI disabled. The config is seeded at the corrected Roaming path so the Web UI is already on and reachable for clients on localhost without a password. The same seed also carries [LegalNotice]\nAccepted=true, matching the key qBittorrent's own src/app/main.cpp checks (CachedSettingValue<bool> legalNoticeShown {"LegalNotice/Accepted", false}) before showing its first-run legal-notice QMessageBox -- on the non-headless Windows GUI build that dialog is always shown and always blocks (isInteractive is hardcoded true there), so an unattended install without this seeded line hangs forever waiting for a click nobody can make. qbittorrent.exe itself is a normal (non-headless) build that keeps running in the tray once started; #968's start/poll shape applies here too.

transmission.note: The .msi is a per-machine Windows Installer package: ComponentInstallService runs it through msiexec.exe itself (ALLUSERS=1, a verbose /l*v log next to the download) rather than launching the .msi path directly through ShellExecute's file-type association, which returned exit code 1603 unattended on a clean VM. That same clean VM traced the 1603 to the MSI's own LaunchConditions: it refuses outright with 'The Visual C++ Runtime is not installed or is outdated. Please download and install the latest version from here: https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/vc_redist.x64.exe' when the VC++ 2015-2022 x64 runtime is missing, which a fresh Windows Server image is. The prerequisite installs that redistributable first (skipped when HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\VisualStudio\14.0\VC\Runtimes\x64's own Installed=1 already says it is there), verified by its own Microsoft Authenticode signature since aka.ms is a live redirect with no fixed file to pin a checksum against; exit codes 0 and 3010 (succeeded, reboot required) both count as success, since a plain non-zero/non-3010 exit is the only outcome that should stop Transmission's own install from proceeding. transmission-daemon.exe ships in the same MSI as the Qt client and opens its RPC web interface on 9091 with no extra flags needed.

deluge.note: deluge-torrent/deluge publishes no GitHub Releases (tags only), so the old https://download.deluge-torrent.org/windows/ page URL was never an installer -- it downloaded that page itself, far short of minimumBytes. The real Windows builds are versioned files in a plain directory listing at ftp.osuosl.org (the same host download.deluge-torrent.org serves from), each with its own '<file>.sha256' next to it in the same 'hash  filename' shape as a GitHub SHA256SUMS.txt line, resolved the same way #640/#968 already resolve Weir's latest release, just from a directory listing instead of the GitHub API. Both the 64-bit ('win64') and libtorrent<2.0 compatibility ('win64-lt2.0') builds are published; the pattern picks the plain win64 build. deluged (the torrent daemon) is started untracked ahead of deluge-web (the Web UI/API Deluno talks to on 8112); deluge-web comes up and answers even before a host is added in it, but full transfers need deluged already reachable -- unverified without a real VM.

sabnzbd.configFileContent:
[misc]
host = 0.0.0.0
port = 8080
host_whitelist = 
enable_https = 0
api_key = 
username = 
password = 

[categories]
sabnzbd.note: Keeps SABnzbd's own default port 8080; qBittorrent moves to 8081 instead so the two never clash. The seeded ini and --browser 0 are meant to skip SABnzbd's first-run setup wizard (which otherwise opens a browser and waits for answers no unattended install can give) and to blank the host whitelist so a loopback API call is accepted -- unverified without a real VM; #968 stays open if a live run still shows the wizard.

nzbget.note: The old url was the GitHub releases *page* (https://github.com/nzbget/nzbget/releases/latest), not an asset -- it downloaded ~214KB of HTML, nowhere near minimumBytes. NZBGet does publish real GitHub Releases, unlike Deluge, so this resolves the same way Weir does: latest release, asset name matched by pattern since it embeds the version (nzbget-21.1-bin-windows-setup.exe), excluding the '-debug-' build. The clean-VM refusal ('not Authenticode-signed and carries no pinned checksum') was wrong to treat as a dead end: nzbget's release does publish a checksum file per version, named nzbget-<version>.sig.txt (e.g. nzbget-21.1.sig.txt, fetched and confirmed over HTTPS from github.com/nzbget/nzbget/releases -- not a SHA256SUMS.txt, so it needs its own name pattern the same way the installer asset itself does), just not the plain 'hash  filename' shape GithubLatestRelease.ParseChecksum already reads for Weir/Deluge. It is instead a JSONP body, `nzbget_signatures({ "SHA256(nzbget-21.1-bin-windows-setup.exe)" : "<hash>", ... });`, so ParseChecksum now also recognises that shape. mustBeSigned still stays on as a fallback for the rare release that omits the file. '-D' runs NZBGet as a background daemon; its default nzbget.conf already opens the control (Web UI/API) port 6789 on loopback with no extra flags.

weir.note: Weir is Deluno's own sibling product, not a third-party download client. Its Windows installer publishes SHA256SUMS.txt with every GitHub release, so its own release is checked against its own published hash rather than one pinned here. Per Weir's own docs/release.md ('Installing Weir from another program'): the Setup's --silent installs and exits (it does not start Weir); Weir.exe is then started separately as the installing user's tray app, not a service; and readiness is polled at /ready rather than waited on via the process tree, because Weir.exe keeps running after it is ready.
